analysis.one_liner: Gradually raises the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour and ends every subminimum wage.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on April 28, 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote has taken place since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal wage law in three big steps. First, it raises the federal minimum wage on a fixed schedule to $25 an hour by 2031 for large companies ($1 billion in revenue or 500+ employees) and by 2038 for everyone else, then ties the minimum to two-thirds of the national median wage so it rises automatically with the economy [S2]. Second, it phases out the separate lower wages now allowed for tipped workers, newly hired teens, workers with disabilities in certified "sheltered" jobs, and incarcerated workers [S2]. Third, it sets the future minimum as a fixed share of what typical workers earn, so it can no longer sit frozen for a decade as prices climb [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers at the bottom of the pay scale gain most directly: everyone earning under $25 an hour, tipped servers and restaurant staff, teenagers in their first jobs, workers with disabilities paid special certificate wages, and incarcerated workers, who would count as employees for the first time under federal wage law. Workers in the roughly 30 states where the minimum is still $7.25-$15 gain the most, since their employers could not pay below the new schedule. The bill's own findings argue higher wages would also reduce reliance on public assistance programs [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage, tipped, disabled, and incarcerated workers

how_it_helps.text: Large employers must raise their minimum from $12 to $25 an hour by January 1, 2031; other employers get a slower schedule reaching $25 by 2038 [S2].
The bill defines 'large employer' as any company with $1 billion or more in annual revenue or 500 or more employees nationwide, so the biggest and most profitable companies move first [S2].

Once the schedule is complete, the minimum wage is automatically adjusted each year to stay at two-thirds of the national median hourly wage, ending the pattern of the minimum losing value between acts of Congress [S2].

The tipped minimum wage (now $2.13) phases out: tipped workers at large employers reach the full minimum within five years of the effective date, and all tipped workers eventually get the same floor as everyone else, with a new right to keep their tips [S2].

The separate youth subminimum (now $4.25 for new hires under 20) is phased out and then repealed, and the section 14(c) program that lets employers pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum is phased out, with no new special certificates allowed and a sunset written into law [S2].

Incarcerated workers, including people working for private prison operators or in UNICOR and state prison industries, are brought under the Fair Labor Standards Act for the first time, and amounts deducted for room, board, or court-imposed fees cannot be counted as wages [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and franchise chains pay the biggest wage bills, with the schedule starting at $12 an hour and climbing to $25 by 2031 [S2]. The restaurant industry absorbs a structural change: the two-tier tipped wage system ends, meaning table service must be covered by the regular minimum [S2]. Employers holding section 14(c) certificates and private prison operators lose their access to labor below the wage floor [S2]. Small businesses get a longer runway but the same $25 endpoint by 2038. Some employers would pass higher labor costs to consumers through prices; some economists argue steep increases can also cost jobs or hours, particularly in lower-wage regions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations, restaurant chains, prison operators

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a single national wage floor with no regional cost-of-living adjustment, so a $25 minimum buys very different amounts in a low-cost small town than in an expensive metro, and small employers face the same endpoint as giants, just seven years later [S2].

Economists disagree about how much of a wage increase of this size employers would offset by cutting jobs, hours, or benefits; the Congressional Budget Office has generally found large minimum wage increases raise pay for millions but also cause some job losses, and the steepest steps here fall on large employers by 2031.

The tipped-wage phase-out is a real change in how restaurants operate: full-service restaurants would owe servers the full minimum cash wage even where tips currently push servers well above it, and the industry argues that risks closures and reduced tip income [S2].

Ending the section 14(c) subminimum could eliminate some sheltered jobs rather than convert them, which is why the bill includes transition assistance and a requirement that the Labor Department protect continuing employment opportunities for workers with disabilities [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and specific: millions of workers would see their pay floor rise far faster than the current $7.25 federal minimum, and four groups now legally paid less than the minimum would get the full floor for the first time. The costs are real but standard for this kind of policy: businesses bear higher payrolls, some of it lands on consumers as prices, and the risk of job or hour losses in the lowest-wage markets is the honest unknown. The two-tier design (big companies first, small ones later) and the automatic median-wage indexing reduce the shock compared with an immediate jump. The main design weakness is the flat national floor with no regional adjustment.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 28, 2026 and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no further action, so it sits there with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the Living Wage For All Act in the House on April 28, 2026 [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day [S4].
Thirty-two House Democrats are cosponsors; no Republican or Independent is listed [S3].
No committee action, floor vote, or Senate companion has appeared in the record since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers paying less than the bill's schedule are better off, because the bill has not moved and no wage requirements have come into effect; no one has had to change anything yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping the wage status quo

for.name: Rep. Delia Ramirez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Living Wage For All Act on April 28, 2026.

for.name: 32 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up its entire listed support.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has joined, and the House Education and Workforce Committee, which Republicans chair, has taken no action since the referral [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Large low-wage employers (big-box retail, fast food and franchise chains, logistics)
industries.note: Companies with $1 billion in revenue or 500+ employees face the fastest schedule, reaching $25 an hour by 2031, and the bill's findings explicitly say they have the greatest capacity to pay and must lead the transition [S2]. Their interest in keeping the current federal minimum runs against the wage gains the bill delivers to their employees.

The bill phases out the tipped minimum wage, so restaurants must pay servers the full regular minimum, converting a tip-subsidized wage structure into a straight wage [S2]. Servers get a stronger guaranteed floor; restaurants bear higher payroll costs.

The program allowing subminimum wages for workers with disabilities is phased out, no new certificates may be issued, and the authority sunsets once wage rates converge [S2]. Workers with disabilities gain the full minimum; certificate-holding employers lose their below-minimum labor model.

industries.industry: Private prison operators and prison industry programs
industries.note: Incarcerated workers are brought under the Fair Labor Standards Act for the first time, including people working for private contractors, UNICOR, and state prison industries, and room, board, and court-fee deductions no longer count as wages [S2]. Private operators lose access to labor outside the wage floor.
They get seven extra years, not reaching $25 until 2038, and start at the same $12 floor, so the transition is cushioned but the endpoint is the same higher payroll cost [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With 32 of 217 House Democrats supporting and a committee controlled by the 223-member Republican majority showing no action since the referral, the likely path is that the bill receives no hearing or markup and dies at the end of this Congress without a vote, as most minimum-wage bills introduced by the minority party do.
